rungs.stem: In the Old English poem Beowulf, the hero has grown old. Fifty years after tearing off Grendel's arm in the Danish mead-hall Heorot, Beowulf has been the king of the Geats for a long time, ruling in peace. Then trouble comes to his own land -- a runaway slave stumbles into a barrow-mound on a headland and steals one bright thing from a hoard guarded by a sleeping monster. What does the slave steal from the hoard?
rungs.context: Beowulf 2214-2231. The fleeing slave picks up a single golden cup from the pile and creeps back out of the mound. When the monster wakes and counts his gold and finds the cup gone, he goes berserk. Every other detail is a real Anglo-Saxon treasure motif -- helmets, rings, and daggers all appear elsewhere in the poem -- but the specific stolen item is the cup.

rungs.stem: The monster in the barrow whose hoard was robbed of the golden cup wakes up furious. That very night he uncoils, flies out over the countryside of Geatland breathing fire, and burns down one specific building of the king's -- an insult none of the Geats will forgive. What does the dragon burn down that first night?
rungs.context: Beowulf 2302-2323. The dragon burns Beowulf's own royal hall to the ground -- the poet marks it as the personal insult that drives Beowulf, now old, to arm one last time and ride out. The watchtower, the ships, and any temple all appear elsewhere in Anglo-Saxon material, but the dragon's first burning is the king's hall.

rungs.stem: Beowulf is now an old man, and he knows a wooden linden-shield -- the ordinary shield of every Geat warrior -- will simply catch fire against dragon-flame. So he orders a shield made specially for this fight, of a different material altogether, so it will not burn. What is the special shield Beowulf orders for the dragon-fight made of?
rungs.context: Beowulf 2337-2341. The poet stresses that Beowulf's usual linden-wood shield would be useless against flame, so he commissions an iron shield for the ride out to the mound. Boiled leather is real Anglo-Saxon armour but never a shield-material for this fight; yew is a wood (so it would burn); bronze belongs to Bronze-Age heroes, not Beowulf's Migration-era Geatland. The dragon-fight shield is iron.

rungs.stem: Beowulf rides to the barrow with a war-band -- but only a small one. The poet names the count exactly, so the coming shame will land hard. How many thanes does Beowulf take with him to the mound to fight the dragon?
rungs.context: Beowulf 2401-2405. He takes eleven thanes with him -- twelve fighters counting the king himself. The number is set up carefully so that the poet can later tell you EXACTLY how many run (ten) and exactly how many stay (one), and the arithmetic is the shame. Small war-bands appear elsewhere in the poem in threes and larger hosts in the fifties or hundreds; this specific ride to the mound is eleven.

rungs.stem: At the barrow, Beowulf shouts a war-cry down into the mouth of the mound and the dragon comes rushing out breathing fire. Beowulf swings his old sword against the dragon's scaled head -- but the sword lets him down. In one of Beowulf's most-quoted lines, 'the blade failed him in the fight; his old iron was not fated to help him.' What is the name of Beowulf's own sword in the dragon-fight?
rungs.context: Beowulf 2679-2687. Naegling is Beowulf's own famous blade -- and it shatters in his grip when it bites too shallow on the dragon's scales. Hrunting was Unferth's sword, which had failed Beowulf earlier against Grendel's mother in the mere; the giant-forged wall-sword in that mere-cave was unnamed and melted in the monster's blood. Nothung and Balmung are the German sword-names from Wagner's Ring cycle and the Nibelungenlied for Sigurd's / Siegfried's sword, not Beowulf's.

rungs.stem: Once Beowulf's sword shatters, the dragon closes in and does one very specific thing that will kill the old king in the end. He does not burn Beowulf, and he does not crush him. What does the dragon do?
choices: fastens his fangs in Beowulf's throat
lifts him into the air by the shield
rungs.answer: fastens his fangs in Beowulf's throat
rungs.context: Beowulf 2688-2705. The dragon sinks his fangs into Beowulf's neck -- and along with the bite comes the venom that will kill the king even after the dragon is dead. Everything else the dragon does in the poem (breathing fire, coiling on the hoard, flying with wings) is real, but the specific killing wound is the fanged bite to the throat.

rungs.stem: Of the eleven thanes Beowulf brought, ten turn and run into the woods when the flame comes. Only ONE thane -- a young kinsman of Beowulf who has never fought a battle before this day -- runs INTO the fire beside his falling king and helps him kill the dragon. What is the loyal thane's name?
rungs.context: Beowulf 2596-2601. Wiglaf, son of Weohstan, of the Waegmunding clan and Beowulf's own kinsman, is the one thane who does not flee. His Old English name means 'battle-remnant' or 'battle-heir' -- the one who stays behind after the others are gone. Hondscioh was the Geat Grendel devoured first in Heorot fifty years earlier; Aeschere was Hrothgar's counsellor, killed by Grendel's mother; Hygelac was Beowulf's own late king back in Geatland. The one who stays with Beowulf against the dragon is Wiglaf.

rungs.stem: Wiglaf drives his sword up into the dragon's softer lower body where the scales are thin, and the flames drop. Then Beowulf himself, dying from the throat-wound but still on his feet, draws a shorter weapon from his belt and finishes the dragon in one specific way. What does Beowulf do with his belt-knife?
choices: cuts the dragon in half at the middle
drives it through the dragon's eye
buries it in the dragon's tongue
wedges it in the dragon's jaws
rungs.answer: cuts the dragon in half at the middle
rungs.context: Beowulf 2699-2705. With Wiglaf's sword-thrust already inside the dragon, Beowulf pulls his war-knife and cuts the beast in two at the belly. The dragon dies between them. The eye-thrust belongs to Odysseus and Polyphemus in the Greek Odyssey; the tongue and the jaws are common dragon-slaying motifs but not Beowulf's move. The specific finish is the knife across the middle.

rungs.stem: Dying beside the dead dragon, Beowulf gives Wiglaf one specific request before the venom finishes him. It is not about vengeance on the ten who ran, and it is not about his succession. It is about the gold. What does the dying Beowulf ask Wiglaf to do?
choices: bring out some of the treasure so he can see it
carry his war-knife back to the queen
burn the dragon's body on the mound
spare the ten thanes who fled
rungs.answer: bring out some of the treasure so he can see it
rungs.context: Beowulf 2743-2820. The old king asks Wiglaf to go into the barrow and bring out some of the dragon's hoarded gold so he can look on the treasure he won for his people before he dies. Wiglaf does it -- he carries out cups and standards and lays them at his king's feet, and Beowulf sees the gold and gives thanks and dies. The last of the ten cowards is dealt with LATER by Wiglaf, not by Beowulf; the funeral is arranged later; the war-knife stays with the body.

rungs.stem: The Geats burn Beowulf on a great pyre and raise a burial-mound over his ashes on a specific headland, so tall that every ship going by at sea will see it and remember him. The Old English name of the headland is a compound name; the second half is the ordinary Old English word for a sea-cliff or headland. What is the name of Beowulf's burial-place?
rungs.context: Beowulf 3136-3155. Hronesnaess (Old English hron 'whale' + ness 'headland') is the sea-cliff where the pyre is built and the mound is raised. Earnanaess ('Eagle's-Ness') is the earlier location, where the dragon's barrow was; Heorot is Hrothgar's Danish mead-hall from Beowulf's youth; Geatasfeld is not a place-name in the poem. The specific burial-headland is Hronesnaess.

rungs.stem: Around Beowulf's finished burial-mound at Hronesnaess, a picked band of warriors -- 'brave in battle, sons of noblemen' -- ride round and round the mound singing dirges and reciting his praises. The poet gives their exact number. How many horsemen ride around the mound?
rungs.context: Beowulf 3169-3177. Twelve of the best Geat warriors ride round the mound, voicing their grief and speaking Beowulf's deeds aloud so the sound would rise. The circling-praise image is one of the most-copied endings in Old English studies. Seven, three, and twenty-four all appear in other Anglo-Saxon and Old Norse ceremonies but the number of horsemen at this specific mound is twelve.

rungs.stem: The very last word of the Beowulf poem -- lofgeornost -- is one of the most-quoted words in all of Old English literature. The full closing line calls Beowulf the mildest of the world's kings, the gentlest, the kindest to his people, and one thing more. The word lofgeornost means 'keenest for' what?
rungs.context: Beowulf 3182: 'lofgeornost' -- Old English lof ('praise, fame') + geornost ('most eager'). The line says Beowulf was 'of the world's kings the mildest of men and gentlest, kindest to his people, and keenest for praise.' Scholars still argue whether that final word is admiring (a hero's rightful hunger for lasting fame) or a small pointed criticism (a king who cared what people said of him too much); either way, praise is what the last word names, not gold or peace or wisdom.
